en.title: Radiography: the whole course
en.short: How radiography is organised, from anatomy and physics to imaging practice, and how to study it.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text: These notes teach the concepts of radiography. They are not medical advice and do not replace your teachers, textbooks, local protocols or official guidance. They give no drug doses. Imaging and radiotherapy protocols change and differ between countries, so check the current national guidance or World Health Organization (WHO) guidance. Radiation protection rules are set by national regulators. Never use these notes to justify exposing a person to radiation or to interpret a real patient’s image. Only qualified professionals may do that, under local rules and supervision.

sections.heading: What radiography is
sections.text:
Radiography is the health profession that uses X-rays and other imaging methods to look inside the body. Therapeutic radiography uses radiation to plan and deliver treatment for cancer. Diagnostic radiographers produce images that help clinicians detect injury and disease. Therapeutic radiographers work with oncology teams to treat cancer with radiation. In many countries these are separate degrees and registrations.

Radiography joins anatomy, physics, technology, patient care and ethics. A radiographer must know how an image is formed, how to position the patient, how to keep doses as low as reasonably achievable, and how to communicate with people who may be anxious or in pain. The work also includes quality assurance, image interpretation within scope, and teamwork with doctors, nurses and physicists.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Programmes differ by country and institution. Awards include bachelor’s degrees, diplomas and master’s entry routes. In Nigeria, radiography is regulated by the Radiographers Registration Board of Nigeria (RRBN); check current RRBN requirements and your university handbook. In the United Kingdom, diagnostic and therapeutic radiography are usually separate three-year BSc (Hons) degrees with clinical placements, regulated by the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC).

Most courses begin with basic sciences: anatomy, physiology, medical terminology, mathematics and physics. They then move to imaging science, equipment, patient care, radiation protection and clinical placements. Supervised practice in a hospital or clinic is central. You cannot learn positioning or patient communication from books alone. Registration and internship rules change, so confirm them with your national regulator.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually starts with the profession and its scope, medical terminology and anatomical language. Anatomy and physiology follow, first the musculoskeletal system, then the thorax, abdomen and pelvis. Mathematics, radiation physics and atomic structure, and electricity and X-ray circuit basics give the physical foundation. Patient care, communication, infection prevention and patient safety run alongside.

The core covers X-ray production and the X-ray tube, image formation and quality, digital radiography and picture archiving and communication systems (PACS). Radiation biology, protection and dosimetry are taught early because safety shapes every examination. Positioning follows: appendicular skeleton, axial skeleton, skull and facial bones, chest and abdomen. Contrast media, fluoroscopy and interventional radiography come next, with cross-sectional anatomy.

Modality subjects then include computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasound, nuclear medicine and mammography. Pathology, image interpretation and clinical reasoning, quality assurance and equipment, and professional practice, law and ethics complete the core. Master’s level adds advanced imaging physics, research methods and a dissertation, and artificial intelligence in medical imaging.

sections.heading: How to study radiography
sections.text:
Learn the normal before the abnormal. Draw bones, joints and organs from memory, and link each view to the anatomy it shows. In physics, work through calculations such as the inverse square law and attenuation with units written down. Ask what each control on the X-ray console changes and why.

Practise positioning as a sequence: patient preparation, identification, positioning, exposure factors, image check and aftercare. Use simulation and supervised practice. Test yourself with past questions and image sets. Keep a log of cases and errors, and review it. Study radiation protection as a habit, not a topic for one examination.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often memorise exposure factors without understanding image quality, or learn positioning without checking patient safety and consent. Some ignore infection prevention because it seems unrelated to imaging. Others treat radiation protection as paperwork and forget time, distance and shielding in practice.

A common error is to interpret images beyond your scope or to present a finding as a diagnosis. Another is to quote one country’s protocol as universal. In exams, read the question’s setting and available equipment. Finally, do not use notes such as these to advise or image a real person. Work under supervision and follow local rules.

keyPoints: Radiography uses X-rays and other imaging methods safely to diagnose and treat disease.
Radiography degrees combine anatomy, physics, patient care and supervised clinical practice.
Radiation protection and dose reduction are central to every examination.
Learn normal anatomy and physics first, then positioning and image quality.
Protocols, registration rules and equipment differ by country and change over time, so check current official guidance.
These notes teach concepts and are not medical advice.

en.title: Radiography as a profession: history, roles and scope
en.short: What radiography is, its modalities, and the roles and regulation of the imaging team.

sections.heading: What radiography is
sections.text:
Radiography is the use of X-rays and other imaging methods to make pictures of the body for diagnosis and treatment planning. It is also a health profession with its own training and standards. A modality is one imaging method. Main modalities include plain radiography (standard X-ray pictures), fluoroscopy (real-time X-ray imaging), computed tomography (CT, cross-sectional X-ray images), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI, using magnetic fields and radio waves), ultrasound (using sound waves) and nuclear medicine (using radioactive tracers).

Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895, and images of bones followed soon after. The profession grew from film processing in darkrooms to digital image capture and storage.

sections.heading: The imaging team
sections.text:
The radiographer, called a medical radiation technologist in some countries, performs the examination, cares for the patient, positions the patient, selects technical factors (the exposure settings), checks image quality and applies radiation protection. The radiologist is a doctor who interprets images and performs some image-guided procedures. The medical physicist advises on radiation physics, equipment, dosimetry, the measurement of radiation dose, and quality assurance, regular checks that equipment is safe and accurate.

For example, after a road crash in Ibadan, Tunde has an ankle X-ray. A radiographer explains the procedure and obtains the image; a radiologist reports it; a medical physicist may have checked the equipment.

sections.heading: Registration and scope
sections.text:
Professional bodies, registration and scope of practice vary by country. In Nigeria, the Radiographers Registration Board of Nigeria regulates radiographers. In the United Kingdom, the Health and Care Professions Council regulates radiographers, and the Society of Radiographers is a professional body. In the United States, the American Registry of Radiologic Technologists certifies radiologic technologists, while state licensure varies. These arrangements can change, so check the current national regulator.

Scope also varies: after extra training, some radiographers perform ultrasound, mammography, image reporting (interpreting images and writing reports) or radiotherapy; others do not. Follow local law, employer policy and your training.

keyPoints: Radiography uses X-rays and other modalities to image the body for diagnosis and treatment planning.
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895.
The radiographer performs the examination, cares for the patient and applies radiation protection.
The radiologist is a doctor who interprets images and performs some image-guided procedures.
The medical physicist advises on radiation physics, equipment, dosimetry and quality assurance.
Registration, professional bodies and scope of practice vary by country, so check the current national regulator.

en.title: Medical terminology and anatomical language
en.short: Medical word parts and the anatomical terms used to describe positions and images.

sections.heading: Word parts
sections.text: Medical terms are built from roots, prefixes and suffixes. A root gives the main meaning: gastr means stomach, hepat means liver, oste means bone. A prefix comes before the root: hyper means above or excessive, hypo means below or deficient, brady means slow, tachy means fast. A suffix comes after the root: itis means inflammation, megaly means enlargement, oma means tumour, ectomy means surgical removal. So gastritis is stomach inflammation, hepatomegaly is liver enlargement, and osteoma is a bone tumour. Learn the parts and check terms in a medical dictionary.

sections.heading: Position and planes
sections.text: Anatomical position is the standard starting point: standing erect, feet together, arms at the sides, palms forward, head facing forward. Directions are described as if the body is in this position. A plane is a flat surface that divides the body. The median or midsagittal plane divides it into left and right halves. The coronal or frontal plane divides it into anterior and posterior parts. The transverse or axial plane divides it into superior and inferior parts. An oblique plane is slanted. Radiographers use these terms in positioning and image description.

sections.heading: Directions and regions
sections.text: Directional terms compare two points. Superior means nearer the head, inferior nearer the feet. Anterior means nearer the front, posterior nearer the back. Medial means nearer the midline, lateral farther from it. Proximal means nearer the trunk or origin, distal farther away. Superficial means nearer the surface, deep farther inside. Regions name areas: the abdomen is often divided into four quadrants or nine regions, such as the epigastric and umbilical regions. Use the patient’s right and left, not the viewer’s.

sections.heading: Cavities and example
sections.text: Body cavities protect organs. The dorsal cavity contains the cranial and vertebral cavities. The ventral cavity contains the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities, separated by the diaphragm. PA wrist means posteroanterior: the beam enters posterior and exits anterior. Ada reads right wrist as the patient’s right.

keyPoints: Roots give the main meaning; prefixes and suffixes modify it.
Anatomical position is erect, feet together, arms at the sides, palms forward.
Median, coronal and transverse planes divide the body into left/right, anterior/posterior and superior/inferior parts.
Directional terms include superior/inferior, anterior/posterior, medial/lateral, proximal/distal and superficial/deep.
The dorsal cavity contains cranial and vertebral cavities; the ventral cavity contains thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities.
Use the patient’s right and left when describing radiographs.

en.title: Anatomy and physiology of the musculoskeletal system
en.short: Bones, joints, muscles and landmarks: normal structure, growth and radiographic appearance.

sections.heading: Bones and growth
sections.text:
Bone is living tissue. Collagen in its matrix gives tensile strength; calcium phosphate mineral gives stiffness and makes bone radiopaque (white on radiographs). Compact bone forms the outer cortex; cancellous bone is a trabecular network inside. The periosteum covers bone and supplies blood and new bone. Osteoblasts build bone, osteoclasts resorb it, and osteocytes maintain it.

Long bones grow at the physis (growth plate) by endochondral ossification: cartilage is replaced by bone. The diaphysis is the shaft, the metaphysis the flared end, and the epiphysis the articular end. Flat bones such as the skull vault form by intramembranous ossification. Growth plates are radiolucent in children and close by adulthood.

sections.heading: Joints muscles connective tissue
sections.text:
A joint is where bones meet. Fibrous joints, such as skull sutures, allow little movement. Cartilaginous joints, such as those between vertebral bodies (the intervertebral discs), allow limited movement. Synovial joints have a cavity, cartilage and fluid, and allow free movement. Types include hinge, ball-and-socket, pivot, saddle, plane and condyloid; joint shape decides movement range.

Skeletal muscle produces movement and attaches to bone by tendons. Smooth muscle moves substances through organs; cardiac muscle pumps the heart. Ligaments bind bone to bone, fascia wraps muscles, and cartilage covers joint surfaces. These soft tissues are less radiopaque than bone, so they are seen mainly by outline or on other imaging.

sections.heading: Landmarks and normal images
sections.text:
Surface landmarks are named bumps, ridges and hollows: a tuberosity or tubercle is a rounded projection, a condyle is a rounded articular end, an epicondyle lies beside it, a facet is a small flat surface, a foramen is a hole, and a fossa is a hollow. Radiographic landmarks are these features seen as lines and shadows.

Normal bone is white because mineral blocks X-rays; air is black and soft tissue grey. In a teaching case, a 10-year-old’s wrist radiograph shows a dark line across the distal radius. The student should recognise the normal physis at that age, compare views, and not call it a fracture without evidence. Appearance varies with age, projection and exposure, so compare with normal images.

keyPoints: Bone is radiopaque because calcium phosphate mineral blocks X-rays; soft tissue is less dense and air is black.
Long bones grow at the physis by endochondral ossification, and growth plates are normal radiolucent lines in children.
Joint type follows structure: fibrous and cartilaginous joints move little, while synovial joints move freely.
Tendons attach muscle to bone, ligaments attach bone to bone, and cartilage covers joint surfaces.
Surface landmarks such as tuberosity, condyle, facet and foramen appear as characteristic lines and shadows on radiographs.
Normal appearance changes with age, projection and exposure, so compare with normal reference images before calling a feature abnormal.

en.title: Anatomy and physiology of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis
en.short: Normal thorax, abdomen and pelvis: organs, surface anatomy and radiographic landmarks.

sections.heading: Thoracic cavity
sections.text:
The thorax is the chest cavity. The mediastinum is the central space between the lungs; it contains the heart, great vessels, trachea and oesophagus. The heart lies in the middle mediastinum, mostly left of midline. The lungs sit in the pleural cavities; the right lung has three lobes, the left two. The trachea divides at the carina. The diaphragm separates thorax from abdomen.

Surface landmarks include the sternal notch, sternal angle, xiphoid process and costal margin. On a chest image, look for the carina, hila, heart borders, costophrenic angles and diaphragm. The right hemidiaphragm lies higher.

sections.heading: Abdominal organs
sections.text:
The abdomen holds the digestive organs. The liver lies in the right upper quadrant under the right hemidiaphragm. The gallbladder sits under the liver. The stomach and spleen are in the left upper quadrant. The small intestine lies centrally; the colon frames it. The kidneys are retroperitoneal, roughly T12 to L3; the right kidney is slightly lower because of the liver.

Surface landmarks include the costal margin, umbilicus and iliac crests. On an abdominal image, landmarks include the gastric bubble, liver shadow, psoas shadows, renal outlines and bowel gas. For example, on an image of a young woman named Amina, the gastric bubble lies under the left hemidiaphragm and the liver shadow fills the right upper quadrant.

sections.heading: Biliary and pelvic
sections.text:
The biliary system carries bile from the liver to the duodenum. Right and left hepatic ducts form the common hepatic duct. The cystic duct from the gallbladder joins it to form the common bile duct, which opens into the duodenum. The urinary tract includes kidneys, ureters and bladder. The bladder lies in the pelvis behind the pubic symphysis. The rectum lies behind the bladder.

In females the uterus lies between bladder and rectum; in males the prostate lies below the bladder. Surface landmarks include the anterior superior iliac spines and pubic symphysis. On pelvic images, identify the sacrum, pelvic ring, obturator foramina and bladder shadow.

keyPoints: The mediastinum is the central thoracic space containing the heart, great vessels, trachea and oesophagus.
The right lung has three lobes and the left two; the trachea divides at the carina.
The liver and gallbladder lie in the right upper quadrant; the stomach and spleen lie in the left upper quadrant.
The kidneys are retroperitoneal, roughly T12 to L3, and the right kidney is slightly lower.
The common bile duct is formed by the common hepatic duct and cystic duct and opens into the duodenum.
In the pelvis the bladder is anterior, the rectum posterior, and the uterus or prostate lies between or below.

en.title: Mathematics for radiography
en.short: Covers SI units, decimals, fractions, percentages, ratios, exposure time, magnification, inverse square law and graphs.

sections.heading: Units and numbers
sections.text: Radiography uses SI units: metre (m) for distance, kilogram (kg) for mass and second (s) for time. Prefixes change unit size: 1 cm = 0.01 m, 1 mm = 0.001 m, and 1 ms = 0.001 s. A decimal is a fraction written with a point: 0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4. A percentage is a fraction of 100, so 75% = 75/100 = 0.75. A ratio compares quantities, such as 3:1. A proportion states that two ratios are equal. Convert to the same unit before calculating.

sections.heading: Exposure and magnification
sections.text: Exposure time comes from milliampere-seconds (mAs), the product of tube current in milliamperes (mA) and time in seconds: mAs = mA × time. If 20 mAs is needed at 200 mA, time = 20 ÷ 200 = 0.1 s. Magnification compares image size with object size. The factor M = SID ÷ SOD, where SID is source-to-image distance and SOD is source-to-object distance. If SID = 100 cm and SOD = 80 cm, M = 100 ÷ 80 = 1.25. A 5 cm object appears 5 × 1.25 = 6.25 cm long. Keep distances in the same unit.

sections.heading: Inverse square law
sections.text: X-ray intensity falls with distance by the inverse square law: I1 ÷ I2 = (d2 ÷ d1)², where I is intensity and d is distance. If intensity is 400 units at 100 cm, at 200 cm it is 400 × (100 ÷ 200)² = 400 × 0.25 = 100 units. Doubling distance quarters intensity.

sections.heading: Reading graphs
sections.text: Graphs show relationships between two variables. Read the axis labels and units first. The slope of a straight-line graph is change in y ÷ change in x. Interpolation estimates between plotted points; extrapolation estimates beyond them and is less reliable. Check whether the line should pass through zero. For example, mAs against time at fixed mA is a straight line through the origin.

keyPoints: Convert all measurements to the same SI unit before calculating.
mAs = mA × exposure time in seconds.
Magnification factor M = SID ÷ SOD.
Inverse square law: I1 ÷ I2 = (d2 ÷ d1)².
0.25 = 1/4 = 25%, and a ratio such as 3:1 compares two quantities.
On a graph, slope = change in y ÷ change in x; read the axis units first.

en.title: Radiation physics and atomic structure
en.short: Atomic structure, photon energy, ionisation and how X-rays are attenuated in tissue.

sections.heading: Atoms, ionisation and excitation
sections.text:
An atom has a small nucleus of protons (positive) and neutrons (no charge), surrounded by electrons (negative) in shells. The atomic number Z is the number of protons and defines the element. Electrons occupy set energy levels.

If an electron receives enough energy, it leaves the atom. The atom then has a net positive charge and is called an ion; the process is ionisation. If the electron only moves to a higher shell, the atom is excited. It later drops back to its ground state and releases the extra energy, often as light or a characteristic X-ray.

sections.heading: Electromagnetic radiation
sections.text:
Electromagnetic radiation travels as waves and carries energy in packets called photons. Wavelength λ and frequency f are linked by c = f × λ, where c is the speed of light, about 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Photon energy rises with frequency: E = h × f, where h is Planck’s constant, about 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.

Worked example: a photon of frequency 3 × 10¹⁸ Hz has E = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10¹⁸ = 1.99 × 10⁻¹⁵ J. One electron volt is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so this is 1.99 × 10⁻¹⁵ ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 12.4 keV. X-rays are high-frequency, high-energy electromagnetic radiation.

sections.heading: Attenuation and image contrast
sections.text:
As X-rays pass through the body, some photons are absorbed or scattered and the beam is weakened. This is attenuation. In the photoelectric effect the photon is fully absorbed and ejects an inner-shell electron; this is more likely with lower-energy photons and in tissues of higher atomic number, such as bone (calcium) compared with soft tissue. In Compton scattering the photon gives part of its energy to an electron and changes direction; this is more likely at higher energies.

Differences in attenuation between bone, soft tissue and air produce the contrast that forms the image. Attenuation also means dose: absorbed energy can ionise molecules, including DNA, which is the basis of radiation risk. Photons that are not attenuated reach the detector.

keyPoints: Atomic number Z is the number of protons and defines the element.
Ionisation removes an electron from the atom; excitation only raises it to a higher shell.
Photon energy is E = h × f, and c = f × λ.
Photoelectric absorption removes the photon; Compton scattering redirects part of its energy.
Differences in attenuation between bone, soft tissue and air create image contrast.
Absorbed energy causes biological harm, so attenuation links image quality with radiation risk.

en.title: Electricity and X-ray circuit basics
en.short: Current, voltage, resistance, AC and DC, transformers, rectification, X-ray circuits, timing and safety.

sections.heading: Current, voltage, resistance
sections.text:
Electric current is the flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A). Voltage is the potential difference that drives the current, measured in volts (V). Resistance opposes current and is measured in ohms (Ω).

Ohm’s law links them: V = I × R. If 12 V is applied across 3 Ω, then I = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 A. Conductors have low resistance and insulators high resistance. Controlled current and voltage are needed for the X-ray tube and for safety.

sections.heading: AC, DC and transformers
sections.text:
Direct current (DC) flows in one direction, as from a battery. Alternating current (AC) reverses direction many times a second and is the usual mains supply. A transformer changes AC voltage by mutual induction between two coils.

The turns ratio gives Vs ÷ Vp = Ns ÷ Np. A step-up transformer raises voltage and lowers current; a step-down transformer does the opposite. Example: 240 V on a primary of 100 turns and a secondary of 1,000 turns gives 240 × (1,000 ÷ 100) = 2,400 V. Transformers do not work on steady DC.

sections.heading: Rectification and circuit parts
sections.text:
Rectification converts AC to DC using diodes, which allow current mainly in one direction. A bridge full-wave rectifier uses four diodes and gives a smoother output. The high-voltage supply to the X-ray tube is rectified so the anode stays positive relative to the cathode.

A basic X-ray circuit includes the mains supply, fuses or circuit breakers, an exposure switch, a timer, voltage selection, a step-up transformer, a filament step-down transformer, rectifiers, cables and the X-ray tube. Earthing, or grounding, gives fault current a safe path.

sections.heading: Timing and safety
sections.text:
The timer controls exposure length. Accurate timing protects the patient from unnecessary dose and protects the tube from overload. Do not rely on a timer not checked in quality assurance.

Electrical safety includes insulated cables, correct fuses, dry hands and prompt fault reporting. Only trained staff should operate equipment. Electrical and radiation protection rules differ by country; follow your department protocol and current national guidance.

keyPoints: Current is charge flow in amperes; voltage drives it in volts; resistance opposes it in ohms.
Ohm’s law: V = I × R; 12 V across 3 Ω gives 4 A.
DC flows one way; AC reverses direction and is changed by transformers.
Transformer turns ratio: Vs ÷ Vp = Ns ÷ Np; a step-up transformer raises voltage and lowers current.
Rectifiers use diodes to convert AC to DC for the X-ray tube.
Accurate exposure timing and electrical safety protect patient and equipment; follow local national guidance.

en.title: Patient care and communication in radiography
en.short: Communication, consent, privacy, dignity and safe care of anxious, confused or vulnerable patients.

sections.heading: Communication and consent
sections.text:
Communication begins by introducing yourself and your role, checking identity and explaining what will happen and why. Use plain words and an interpreter if needed. Teach-back means asking the patient to repeat the plan in their own words; it shows whether your explanation was clear. Anxiety, confusion and pain reduce understanding, so allow time and check again.

Consent is voluntary agreement to examination or treatment. Informed consent means understanding the purpose, benefits, risks and alternatives. It can be withdrawn at any time. Adults are presumed to have capacity (ability to decide) unless shown otherwise. Laws on consent, children and emergency exceptions differ by country, so follow current national law and professional guidance.

sections.heading: Privacy and dignity
sections.text: Privacy means protecting the person’s body and information from unnecessary exposure. Dignity means treating them as a person, not a condition: cover exposed areas, close curtains, ask before touching, and explain each step. Cultural sensitivity means respecting beliefs, modesty, language, gender preferences and family roles without assuming. Ask who should be present. Record only what is needed and keep images confidential.

sections.heading: Anxiety, confusion and pain
sections.text: Anxious patients need calm, honest information. Confused patients may need a familiar carer, simple orientation and repeated reassurance. Pain makes cooperation harder; ask about it, support the painful part, and pause if needed. Children need age-appropriate words, a parent or carer nearby and distraction. Older people may have hearing, vision or memory problems; face them, speak clearly and allow more time.

sections.heading: Moving and vulnerable adults
sections.text: Before moving anyone, check ability and pain, explain, and get help or equipment. Never drag a patient. Keep them warm and covered. A vulnerable adult is someone less able to protect themselves, such as a frail older person or someone with a disability. Follow safeguarding (protection from harm) policy and report concerns. Case: Mr Okafor, 68, is anxious and hard of hearing before a chest X-ray. The radiographer faces him, speaks slowly, checks identity, explains the position, asks consent, offers privacy, and checks comfort.

keyPoints: Introduce yourself, check identity and explain the examination in plain words.
Teach-back checks understanding by asking the patient to repeat the plan.
Consent must be voluntary and informed, and the patient may withdraw it; follow national law.
Protect privacy and dignity by covering the patient, asking before touching and keeping information confidential.
Anxiety, confusion and pain reduce understanding, so allow time, reassure and pause when needed.
Check ability and pain before moving anyone, use help or equipment, and follow safeguarding policy for vulnerable adults.

en.title: Infection prevention and patient safety in imaging
en.short: Standard precautions, hand hygiene, PPE, waste, isolation, falls, moving, identification and incident reporting.

sections.heading: Standard precautions
sections.text: Standard precautions are basic measures used for every patient, because infection status is often unknown. Treat blood, body fluids, secretions, non-intact skin and mucous membranes as potentially infectious. In imaging this covers patients, linen, equipment and spills. Hand hygiene is the most important measure: clean hands before and after patient contact, after removing gloves, and after touching equipment or waste. Use soap and water when hands are visibly dirty; otherwise an alcohol-based hand rub is suitable. Follow current WHO and national guidance.

sections.heading: PPE, cleaning and waste
sections.text: PPE means gloves, apron or gown, mask and eye protection. Choose by the risk of contact with blood or body fluids; remove it promptly and clean hands. Clean reusable equipment and surfaces between patients, following manufacturer instructions and local policy. Healthcare waste is separated at the point of use: sharps (needles, blades and other sharp items) go into rigid sharps containers, and infectious waste into labelled bags. Never overfill containers. In imaging, contaminated cassettes, detectors and tables need cleaning before the next patient.

sections.heading: Isolation and movement
sections.text: Isolation precautions add transmission-based precautions to standard precautions: contact, droplet or airborne, depending on how the organism spreads. Airborne infections need a respirator, not a plain mask. In imaging, plan the visit, limit staff, put on PPE at the doorway, and clean the room and equipment afterwards. For patient safety, check mobility before transfer. Use brakes, side rails, slide sheets or hoists, and enough staff. Do not lift manually if a safe aid is available. Prevent falls by keeping the patient accompanied and the call bell within reach.

sections.heading: Identification and incidents
sections.text: Identify every patient using at least two identifiers, such as full name and date of birth or hospital number; never use the bed or room number as an identifier. Check before exposure, contrast or procedure. Report incidents and near misses through local reporting, promptly and honestly. A near miss is an event that could have caused harm but did not. Example: a patient slips during transfer but is unharmed; staff assess, record and report it so transfer practice can improve. Follow current national and WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Standard precautions apply to every patient, because infection status may be unknown.
Hand hygiene is the most important single measure; use soap and water when hands are visibly dirty.
PPE is chosen by risk, and reusable equipment and surfaces are cleaned between patients.
Sharps go into rigid containers and infectious waste into labelled bags.
Use at least two patient identifiers and report incidents and near misses promptly.
Check mobility and use safe transfer aids to prevent falls and manual handling injury.

en.title: X-ray production and the X-ray tube
en.short: How X-rays are produced and shaped by tube design, filtration, collimation and exposure factors.

sections.heading: Production and cathode
sections.text: X-rays are made when fast electrons strike a metal target. In the cathode, a tungsten filament is heated. Thermionic emission is the release of electrons from the hot filament. The focusing cup shapes the electron cloud toward the anode. Tube current, in milliamperes (mA), is electron flow per second. Exposure time in seconds multiplied by mA gives mAs, which controls beam quantity. Higher mA releases more electrons, within tube limits.

sections.heading: Anode and focal spot
sections.text: The anode is the target, usually tungsten with rhenium, which resists heat and has a high atomic number. A stationary anode suits low power. A rotating anode spreads heat over a track and allows higher output. The actual focal spot is the area struck by electrons. The effective focal spot is its projected area, smaller because of the line focus principle. A small focal spot improves sharpness but limits mA; a large one handles more heat. The heel effect makes intensity lower on the anode side and higher on the cathode side, so place a thicker part toward the cathode.

sections.heading: Filtration, collimation and spectrum
sections.text: Filtration removes low-energy photons. Inherent filtration comes from the glass envelope and oil; added filtration is usually aluminium. It reduces skin dose and hardens the beam. Collimation limits the field, reduces scatter and dose. The spectrum has a continuous bremsstrahlung part, from electrons slowing in the target, and characteristic peaks, from inner-shell electron ejection. kVp sets maximum photon energy and penetrability. mA and time set quantity. Filtration and voltage waveform change spectrum shape. Too low kVp gives poor penetration and high contrast; too high kVp lowers contrast. Local standards vary, so check current national guidance.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Worked example: if exposure at 100 cm is 10 mAs and distance rises to 200 cm, intensity falls to one quarter by the inverse square law. To keep exposure, mAs must rise fourfold: 10 × 4 = 40 mAs. Check: 200 ÷ 100 = 2, and 2² = 4.

keyPoints: Thermionic emission releases electrons from the heated cathode filament; mA controls tube current and mAs = mA × time controls beam quantity.
The anode target is usually tungsten with rhenium; rotating anodes spread heat and allow higher output.
Actual focal spot is the electron strike area; effective focal spot is smaller by the line focus principle, improving sharpness.
The heel effect lowers intensity on the anode side, so place thicker body parts toward the cathode.
Filtration removes low-energy photons and hardens the beam; collimation limits field size and reduces scatter and dose.
kVp sets maximum photon energy and penetrability; the spectrum has continuous bremsstrahlung and characteristic peaks; inverse square law I1/I2 = (d2/d1)².

en.title: Radiographic image formation and image quality
en.short: How attenuation, exposure factors and geometry shape radiographic contrast, resolution, noise and artefacts.

sections.heading: Attenuation and contrast
sections.text: A radiograph forms because tissues attenuate (reduce) the X-ray beam differently. Differential attenuation is the difference in how much each tissue removes. It depends on thickness, density, atomic number and beam energy. Subject contrast is the range of X-ray intensities leaving the patient; it becomes receptor contrast at the detector. High subject contrast, as between bone and air, gives a clear image. Contrast media increase attenuation. Scattered radiation lowers contrast.

sections.heading: Exposure factors
sections.text: mAs (milliampere-seconds) controls the number of X-ray photons: mAs = mA × time in seconds. More mAs raises receptor exposure and reduces quantum noise, but does not make the beam more penetrating. kVp controls photon energy and penetrability. Higher kVp gives a more penetrating beam, lower subject contrast and more scatter; lower kVp raises contrast but increases dose for the same receptor exposure. Distance follows the inverse square law: exposure falls with the square of distance. Patient size, density and pathology also change attenuation. In digital systems, brightness is a display setting, not a direct measure of dose; receptor exposure must be monitored.

sections.heading: Resolution and geometry
sections.text: Spatial resolution is the ability to separate small adjacent structures, measured in line pairs per millimetre. It improves with a small focal spot, short object-to-detector distance, small pixels and no motion. Distortion is misrepresentation of shape or size. Magnification occurs when the object is far from the detector; shape distortion occurs when the object or beam is angled. Correct positioning and centring reduce it.

sections.heading: Noise and artefacts
sections.text: Noise is unwanted variation that reduces detail. Quantum mottle is noise from too few photons reaching the detector, often after low mAs. Artefacts are false image features from equipment, processing, movement or foreign objects. Example: at 100 cm a detector receives 40 µGy. At 150 cm, exposure = 40 × (100/150)² = 17.8 µGy. To keep exposure, mAs must rise by (150/100)² = 2.25, so 10 mAs becomes 22.5 mAs.

keyPoints: Differential attenuation depends on tissue thickness, density, atomic number and beam energy, and it creates subject contrast.
mAs = mA × time; it controls photon number and receptor exposure, while brightness is a display setting and kVp controls penetrability and scatter.
Exposure follows the inverse square law: new exposure = old exposure × (old distance/new distance)².
Spatial resolution improves with a small focal spot, short object-to-detector distance, small pixels and no motion.
Distortion is shape or size misrepresentation; magnification increases with object-to-detector distance.
Quantum mottle is noise from too few photons; artefacts are false features from equipment, processing, movement or objects.

en.title: Digital radiography, image processing and PACS
en.short: CR and flat-panel detectors, processing, display, DICOM, PACS and dose effects.

sections.heading: Detectors and capture
sections.text: Computed radiography (CR) uses a photostimulable phosphor plate. X-rays store a latent image; a reader scans the plate with laser light and measures the released light. Digital radiography (DR) uses flat-panel detectors. Indirect conversion panels use a scintillator to make light, then photodiodes. Direct conversion panels use a photoconductor, often amorphous selenium, to make charge. Thin-film transistor arrays read the signal. CR plates are reusable but need careful handling and erasure. Flat panels give faster feedback. Pixel size and fill factor affect spatial resolution.

sections.heading: Processing and display
sections.text: Raw digital data need preprocessing: offset, gain and bad-pixel correction. Postprocessing changes display: window and level, edge enhancement and noise reduction. Processing cannot recover missing signal; it can hide under-exposure noise or over-exposure. Display uses medical-grade monitors calibrated to the DICOM grayscale standard display function, with controlled ambient light. Worked example: a 2048 × 2048 image at 16 bits per pixel, 2 bytes, is 2048 × 2048 × 2 = 8,388,608 bytes, about 8 MiB uncompressed, before header and compression. Twelve-bit data are often stored in a 16-bit container.

sections.heading: DICOM, PACS and RIS
sections.text: DICOM is the international standard for image format, metadata and network services. PACS stores, retrieves and displays images. RIS manages orders, scheduling and reports. DICOM worklists link RIS to modalities; HL7 often carries reports. Storage needs backup, audit and retention rules that vary by country. Check local policy and national guidance.

sections.heading: Dose and quality
sections.text: Digital detectors have a wide dynamic range, so exposure errors may be less visible. The exposure index (EI) gives feedback on detector exposure; definitions and targets differ between vendors, though IEC 62494 defines a standardised EI and deviation index. Compare the EI with the manufacturer’s target and local protocol. Dose creep is a risk. Use automatic exposure control and collimation, and monitor repeat and reject rates. Follow current national radiation protection regulations and World Health Organization guidance; protocols differ by country. This is education, not clinical advice.

keyPoints: CR stores a latent image in a phosphor plate; flat-panel detectors convert X-rays to light or charge.
Preprocessing corrects detector artefacts; postprocessing changes display, not the raw data.
File size is approximately matrix width × matrix height × bytes per pixel; 2048 × 2048 × 2 = 8 MiB.
DICOM standardises image format and network services; PACS archives and displays images; RIS manages workflow.
Digital wide dynamic range can hide exposure errors, so use exposure index, AEC and local protocols.
Processing cannot restore missing signal; follow current national and WHO guidance and local policy.

en.title: Radiation biology, protection and dosimetry
en.short: Biological effects, dose quantities, dosimeters, ALARA and shielding for safe radiographic practice.

sections.heading: Biological effects
sections.text: Radiation damages cells directly or indirectly, mainly by ionising water and producing free radicals. DNA damage may be repaired; misrepair can cause mutation or cell death. Deterministic (tissue reaction) effects have a threshold and severity rises with dose, for example skin erythema and cataracts. Stochastic effects, mainly cancer and hereditary effects, are probabilistic; protection assumes risk rises with dose without a threshold. Fetuses and children are more radiosensitive.

sections.heading: Dose quantities
sections.text: Absorbed dose D is the energy absorbed per unit mass. Its unit is the gray (Gy), where 1 Gy = 1 J/kg. Equivalent dose H = D × wR, in sievert (Sv); wR is 1 for X-rays and gamma rays. Effective dose sums tissue equivalent doses weighted by tissue sensitivity and is used for whole-body risk. Example: 0.003 J absorbed in 2 kg gives D = 0.003 ÷ 2 = 0.0015 Gy = 1.5 mGy. For X-rays, the organ equivalent dose is 1.5 mSv.

sections.heading: Dosimeters and ALARA
sections.text: Dosimeters measure personal dose. Film badges darken with dose; thermoluminescent dosimeters (TLD) and optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dosimeters store energy released as light; electronic dosimeters give real-time readings. Wear them as local rules require and review records. ALARA means keeping doses as low as reasonably achievable, with economic and social factors considered. Collimation limits the beam to the area of interest, reducing patient dose and scatter. Shielding includes lead aprons, thyroid shields and barriers; check condition and use correctly.

sections.heading: Protection practice
sections.text: Protection rests on justification, optimisation and dose limitation. Occupational and public dose limits differ by country and are set in national regulations, guided by ICRP recommendations and IAEA safety standards; check the current national regulations rather than memory. Controlled areas have warning signs and local rules. Staff need training and personal monitoring. Public protection uses barriers, distance and restricted access. Pregnant patients and staff need a local risk assessment.

keyPoints: Absorbed dose D = energy absorbed ÷ mass, in gray (Gy); 1 Gy = 1 J/kg.
Equivalent dose H = D × wR, in sievert (Sv); wR is 1 for X-rays and gamma rays.
Deterministic effects have a threshold; stochastic effects are probabilistic and assumed to have no threshold for protection.
ALARA means optimisation using time, distance, shielding and collimation, with economic and social factors considered.
Personal dosimeters include film, TLD, OSL and electronic types; wear and record them as local rules require.
Dose limits differ by country; check current national regulations and ICRP or IAEA guidance.

en.title: Radiography of the appendicular skeleton
en.short: Positioning upper and lower limbs and joints, trauma and routine views, image criteria and protection.

sections.heading: Principles and terms
sections.text: The appendicular skeleton is the bones of the limbs and girdles. A projection is the path of the X-ray beam, such as anteroposterior (AP), posteroanterior (PA), lateral or oblique. A position is how the patient is placed. Identify the part, the joint above and below, and the clinical question. Routine projections usually include two views at right angles; trauma adapts this without moving an injured limb. Check local protocol and current national guidance.

sections.heading: Upper limb
sections.text: Upper limb: fingers, hand, wrist, forearm, elbow, humerus and shoulder. For a finger, centre the affected digit and include the whole digit; for a hand, include the wrist and all fingers; for a forearm, include both wrist and elbow. The two views together show displacement and angulation. For the shoulder, AP and lateral or modified views are used; the exact set depends on suspected injury and local protocol. Collimate to the part and shield where local policy allows.

sections.heading: Lower limb and trauma
sections.text: Lower limb: toes, foot, ankle, lower leg, knee, femur and hip. For a foot, include toes and heel; for an ankle, include distal tibia and fibula; for a knee, include joint space and patella. For a long bone, include the joint above and below. In trauma, do not force a position; use a trolley, supports and a horizontal beam where needed. Example: a student falls and has a painful wrist. Take PA and lateral wrist projections, collimate to the wrist, support the arm, and do not rotate the wrist forcibly. The images must show distal radius and ulna, carpal bones and metacarpal bases.

sections.heading: Criteria and protection
sections.text: Image criteria: all required anatomy included, joints shown, no rotation or movement, correct exposure, no artefacts, and collimation visible. Comfort and immobilisation: explain the procedure, use sponges and sandbags, keep the part still, and respect pain. Radiation protection: ALARA (as low as reasonably achievable), tight collimation, correct exposure, avoid repeats, and follow local shielding and pregnancy policies. Guidelines differ between countries; check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: The appendicular skeleton covers the limb bones and girdles.
A projection is beam direction; a position is patient placement.
Routine limb series usually use two orthogonal views; trauma adapts them to avoid moving the injured part.
For long bones include the joint above and below; for joints include the relevant joint space.
Image criteria include required anatomy, joint spaces, no rotation or movement, correct exposure and no artefacts.
Use ALARA, collimation, immobilisation and local shielding or pregnancy policy, and check current national guidance.

en.title: Radiography of the axial skeleton, skull and facial bones
en.short: Positioning, image criteria and limits for spine, pelvis, skull, facial bones and sinuses.

sections.heading: Terms and principles
sections.text: This topic covers the spine, pelvis, skull and facial bones. A projection is the path of the X-ray beam; a position is how the patient is placed; a view is the resulting image. Centre the beam, collimate to the area of interest, and immobilise only when safe. Image criteria are the checklist for a diagnostic image: full coverage, correct alignment, no rotation, adequate exposure, visible soft tissues and no artefacts. Landmarks guide review: in the spine, the dens, pedicles and spinous processes; in the skull, sutures, sella turcica, orbits and zygomatic arches.

sections.heading: Spine and pelvis
sections.text: For cervical spine trauma, common plain projections are lateral, anteroposterior (AP) and open-mouth odontoid; the lateral should show C1 to T1 when possible. Thoracic and lumbar spine use AP and lateral. Pelvis uses AP, centred on the midline. Image criteria include all vertebrae or the whole pelvis, clear pedicles and spinous processes, open sacroiliac and hip joints, and no rotation. Landmarks include cervical lordosis, the dens, sacral foramina and Shenton line.

sections.heading: Skull, face and sinuses
sections.text: Skull radiography commonly uses posteroanterior (PA), lateral and Towne’s (AP axial) projections. Facial bones use occipitomental (Waters), fronto-occipital and lateral projections; occipitomental also shows the maxillary sinuses. Sinus series vary, but Caldwell, lateral and occipitomental views are common. Image criteria are symmetry, clear orbital margins, visible zygomatic arches, a straight nasal septum and clear sinus margins. Landmarks include sutures, sella turcica, petrous ridges and maxillary antra. Plain sinus films are limited: mucosal thickening and fluid are nonspecific, and CT is better for complex disease.

sections.heading: Trauma and limits
sections.text: Plain radiography shows alignment and obvious fractures but can miss subtle fractures and cannot show cord injury or most soft tissue injury. In significant head, facial or cervical trauma, CT is often first line; guidelines vary. A cyclist with facial swelling may have occipitomental and lateral facial views under local protocol, but suspected orbital or zygomatic complex injury needs CT. Do not use plain films alone to clear the cervical spine in an unconscious or intoxicated patient without local protocol.

keyPoints: A projection is the beam path; a position is the patient’s placement; a view is the image.
Image criteria check coverage, alignment, rotation, exposure, soft tissues and artefacts.
Cervical spine trauma plain series commonly includes lateral, AP and open-mouth odontoid; CT is often first line in significant trauma.
Pelvis AP and spine AP or lateral views need no rotation and clear joints and pedicles.
Occipitomental (Waters) view is used for facial bones and maxillary sinuses; sinus series vary.
Plain radiography cannot exclude subtle fractures or cord injury; follow local protocols.

en.title: Chest and abdominal radiography
en.short: Erect, supine and mobile chest and abdominal radiography: indications, positioning, criteria and normal appearances.

sections.heading: Projections and limits
sections.text: A projection is the path of the X-ray beam through the patient. Erect means upright, supine means lying on the back, and mobile means at the bedside. PA means the beam enters from the back and AP from the front. The erect PA chest is standard for lungs and heart; a lateral view is often added. Supine or mobile AP chest views are used when the patient cannot stand, but the heart looks larger and detail is poorer. For the abdomen, supine AP is common. Erect chest or abdomen may be requested for suspected free gas or obstruction. Mobile views are limited by position, scatter and movement and do not replace CT when CT is needed.

sections.heading: Preparation and protection
sections.text: Check the request and identity, explain the procedure, and remove metal objects that may obscure the image. Ask about pregnancy according to local protocol. Collimate to the area of interest, use the lowest exposure that gives adequate quality, and follow ALARA: keep doses as low as reasonably achievable. Shielding policy varies, so follow current local rules. A carer who supports the patient needs a lead apron and should stay out of the beam. Record repeats and review why they happened.

sections.heading: Positioning and normal
sections.text: For an erect PA chest, the patient faces the detector, chin raised, shoulders forward, beam centred to midline. Criteria: both apices and costophrenic angles included, spine centred, clavicles symmetric, adequate inspiration. For supine abdomen, centre to mid-abdomen and include lower chest to symphysis when acute disease is suspected. Erect abdomen includes diaphragm and pelvis. Check coverage, rotation, exposure and movement. Normal chest shows air-filled lungs, heart, mediastinum, diaphragm and bones. Normal abdomen shows stomach and colon gas, liver shadow, psoas margins, renal outlines and bones. For example, after sudden abdominal pain, an erect chest may show free gas under the diaphragm, but a normal film does not exclude perforation. Guidelines differ; check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Erect PA chest is standard; supine or mobile AP chest is used when the patient cannot stand.
Erect chest or abdomen can help detect free gas or obstruction, but a normal film does not exclude disease.
Collimate, use the lowest adequate exposure, and follow ALARA and local shielding rules.
Check identity, pregnancy status and remove metal objects before exposure.
Image criteria include full coverage, no rotation, adequate inspiration and correct exposure.
Normal chest and abdomen show recognisable gas, soft tissue and bone patterns.

en.title: Contrast media, fluoroscopy and interventional radiography
en.short: Barium and iodinated contrast, safety, reactions, fluoroscopy, angiography and interventional dose care.

sections.heading: Contrast agents and routes
sections.text: Contrast media increase X-ray attenuation differences between tissues. Barium sulphate is a suspension swallowed or given rectally for gastrointestinal studies. It is inert and not absorbed, but must not be used when perforation is suspected because leakage causes peritonitis. Iodinated contrast contains iodine, which attenuates X-rays, and can be given intravenously, intra-arterially, orally, rectally, or into cavities and ducts. Route changes risk: intravascular use can affect kidneys and cause hypersensitivity; oral or rectal use risks aspiration or bowel effects.

sections.heading: Safety checks and reactions
sections.text: Before contrast, confirm identity, procedure, consent, allergy history including previous reaction, asthma, pregnancy, kidney disease, and medicines; check renal function for intravascular iodinated contrast per local policy. Ensure resuscitation equipment and trained staff are available. Reactions range from mild nausea, flushing and urticaria to severe breathing difficulty, low blood pressure and collapse. Contrast-induced acute kidney injury is a separate risk. If a reaction occurs, stop the injection, call for help, assess airway, breathing and circulation, give oxygen, monitor, and follow current local or WHO guidance. Record and report.

sections.heading: Fluoroscopy and angiography
sections.text: Fluoroscopy produces real-time X-ray images, often with a flat-panel detector or image intensifier. It is used for barium studies, catheter placement and image-guided procedures. Angiography uses iodinated contrast to show blood vessels; digital subtraction angiography (DSA) subtracts background structures to make vessels clearer. Basic interventional radiography guides needles, catheters and wires for biopsy, drainage, angioplasty, stenting and embolisation. It is less invasive than open surgery but not risk-free: bleeding, infection, vessel injury and contrast reactions can occur.

sections.heading: Dose awareness and care
sections.text: Fluoroscopy can give high skin doses in long or repeated procedures. Keep screening time and dose as low as reasonably practicable: use pulsed fluoroscopy, collimate, avoid unnecessary magnification, keep the detector close, and use last-image hold. Record dose when required. Explain the procedure, obtain consent, check anticoagulant medicines per local policy, and monitor the puncture site and circulation afterwards. After a long embolisation, staff note the dose and arrange skin follow-up as local policy requires.

keyPoints: Barium sulphate is for gastrointestinal studies and is avoided if perforation is suspected.
Iodinated contrast can be given by several routes; intravascular use carries renal and hypersensitivity risks.
Check identity, allergy history, pregnancy, renal function and resuscitation readiness before contrast.
For a severe reaction, stop contrast, call for help, support airway, breathing and circulation, and follow current local or WHO guidance.
Fluoroscopy is real-time imaging; keep screening time and dose low with pulsed fluoroscopy, collimation and last-image hold.
Interventional procedures are image-guided and minimally invasive but carry bleeding, infection and contrast risks.

en.title: Cross-sectional anatomy for medical imaging
en.short: CT and MRI sectional anatomy of the head, neck, thorax, abdomen and pelvis, including normal variants.

sections.heading: Planes and orientation
sections.text: Cross-sectional anatomy is the study of the body as seen in slices. CT usually acquires axial (transverse) images, and coronal and sagittal views are reconstructed from them; MRI can acquire directly in any plane. In axial images the patient is viewed from below: anterior is at the top, the patient’s right is on the image left. Coronal images are viewed from the front; sagittal images from the side. Recognising these conventions prevents left-right errors. Slice thickness matters: thin slices show small structures, while thick slices blur them through partial volume averaging.

sections.heading: Head and neck
sections.text: The head shows the cerebral lobes, ventricles, basal ganglia, brainstem and cerebellum. The pituitary gland lies in the sella turcica, with the optic chiasm above and the cavernous sinuses beside it. The neck contains the airway, oesophagus, thyroid gland, carotid arteries, jugular veins and cervical spine. Lymph node groups follow the fascial spaces. Common normal variants include a cavum septum pellucidum (a small fluid-filled cavity between the lateral ventricles), a small arachnoid cyst and asymmetric venous sinuses. These must not be mistaken for disease. Midline shift, enlarged ventricles and abnormal extra-axial fluid collections are key abnormalities to recognise.

sections.heading: Thorax, abdomen and pelvis
sections.text: In the thorax, know the mediastinal compartments, great vessels, heart chambers, trachea and main bronchi, oesophagus and lung lobes separated by fissures. The abdomen shows the liver segments, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, kidneys, adrenal glands, bowel, aorta and inferior vena cava. The retroperitoneum lies behind the peritoneal cavity. Organ relationships explain patterns: the pancreas lies in front of the splenic vein, and the left kidney relates to the spleen and pancreatic tail. The pelvis contains the bladder, rectum, uterus and ovaries in women, prostate and seminal vesicles in men, and the pelvic floor and sacrum. Normal variants include an accessory spleen and variant biliary branching; congenital anomalies such as a horseshoe kidney may also be found incidentally. A small case: on axial CT, free gas under the diaphragm suggests a perforated hollow organ; pelvic anatomy also helps trace an appendix that extends down into the pelvis.

keyPoints: Cross-sectional anatomy reads body structures in axial, coronal and sagittal planes.
On axial images, anterior is at the top and the patient’s right is on the image left.
The pituitary lies in the sella turcica, with the optic chiasm above and cavernous sinuses lateral.
Thoracic and abdominal organ relationships explain where fluid, gas and masses spread.
Pelvic anatomy differs by sex and includes the bladder, rectum and reproductive organs.
Normal variants such as cavum septum pellucidum, and congenital anomalies such as horseshoe kidney, should be recognised and not mistaken for disease.

en.title: Computed tomography: physics and practice
en.short: CT tube and detector design, helical scanning, reconstruction, windowing, artefacts, protocols and dose.

sections.heading: Tube and detectors
sections.text: CT uses a rotating X-ray tube and a detector array on the opposite side of the gantry. The tube has a high heat capacity and a small focal spot to balance sharpness and heat. Detectors, often scintillation crystals with photodiodes or semiconductor materials, convert X-rays into electrical signals. Multi-row detectors allow several slices per rotation, thin slices and fast coverage. Collimation defines slice thickness and reduces scatter.

sections.heading: Helical scanning and reconstruction
sections.text: Helical scanning moves the table continuously while the tube rotates, giving a volume of data and reducing motion gaps. Pitch is table travel per rotation divided by the total collimated beam width; a pitch above 1 covers more patient per rotation but can increase noise if other factors are fixed. Reconstruction turns projection measurements into attenuation maps. Filtered back projection applies a filter before back projection to reduce blur. Iterative reconstruction compares predicted with measured projections repeatedly and can lower noise or dose, though it changes image texture.

sections.heading: Windowing and artefacts
sections.text: Windowing maps Hounsfield units (HU) to grey levels. HU = 1000 × (μ_tissue − μ_water) ÷ μ_water. Water is 0 HU and air about −1000 HU. If tissue attenuation is 1.04 times water, HU = 1000 × (1.04 − 1) ÷ 1 = 40. A window level of 40 HU and width of 400 HU displays −160 to 240 HU. Common artefacts include motion, beam hardening, metal streaks, partial volume and rings from detector faults.

sections.heading: Protocols, dose and care
sections.text: Protocol selection depends on the clinical question, body region, patient size and contrast need. Dose optimisation follows justification and optimisation: scan only the needed range, use automatic exposure control, adjust kVp and mAs, and avoid repeats. International bodies such as IAEA, ICRP and WHO publish radiation safety guidance, and national regulators set local requirements; check current national and international guidance rather than a fixed protocol. Patient care includes explanation, consent, pregnancy and allergy checks, breath-hold coaching, comfort and monitoring.

keyPoints: CT pairs a rotating X-ray tube with a detector array; multi-row detectors allow thin slices and fast volume coverage.
Helical scanning acquires a continuous volume; pitch is table travel per rotation divided by total collimated beam width.
Filtered back projection and iterative reconstruction convert projections into attenuation maps; iterative methods can reduce noise or dose.
HU = 1000 × (μ_tissue − μ_water) ÷ μ_water; water is 0 HU and air about −1000 HU.
Windowing sets display contrast and brightness using window level and width; for example level 40 HU and width 400 HU show −160 to 240 HU.
Optimise dose by justifying the scan, limiting range, using automatic exposure control and avoiding repeats; follow current national and international guidance.

en.title: Magnetic resonance imaging: principles and safety
en.short: Magnetism, resonance, gradients, pulse sequences, contrast, artefacts and MRI safety.

sections.heading: Magnetism and resonance
sections.text:
MRI uses a static field, B0, in tesla (T); scanners are often 1.5 T or 3 T. Hydrogen nuclei have spin and are abundant in water and fat. In B0 they precess at the Larmor frequency, f = (γ/2π) × B0, where γ is the gyromagnetic ratio; for hydrogen, γ/2π is about 42.58 MHz per tesla. An RF pulse at this frequency causes resonance, tipping the magnetisation.

After the pulse, T1 describes longitudinal recovery and T2 transverse decay; T2* adds field inhomogeneity. Example: at 1.5 T, f = 42.58 × 1.5 = 63.87 MHz.

sections.heading: Gradients and sequences
sections.text:
Gradient coils create changes in B0 and encode position by slice selection, phase encoding and frequency encoding. RF coils transmit and receive signal; a coil near the body part improves signal-to-noise ratio.

Pulse sequences time RF and gradient events. In spin echo, TR (repetition time) and TE (echo time) set contrast: short TR and short TE give T1 weighting, long TR and long TE give T2 weighting, and long TR with short TE gives proton density weighting. Gradient echo is faster but more sensitive to field inhomogeneity. Fat is bright on T1; fluid is bright on T2.

sections.heading: Common artefacts
sections.text:
Artefacts include motion (blurring or ghosting), chemical shift at fat-water boundaries, susceptibility distortion near metal, aliasing (tissue outside the field of view wraps into the image) and zipper artefact from RF interference.

The cause guides the fix: breath-holding, changed parameters or removing metal.

sections.heading: Safety rules
sections.text:
Safety starts with screening. Ferromagnetic objects can become projectiles: remove keys, scissors and oxygen cylinders. Check implants against manufacturer information: devices are labelled MR safe, MR conditional or MR unsafe. Pacemakers, cochlear implants and aneurysm clips need particular care. RF energy can heat tissue, measured as specific absorption rate (SAR); gradients cause acoustic noise and nerve stimulation. A quench releases cryogen gas, so follow evacuation procedures.

In pregnancy, MRI without contrast may be used when clinically needed, but practice varies, especially in the first trimester; gadolinium is usually avoided unless essential. Check current national and local guidance.

keyPoints: The Larmor frequency is f = (γ/2π) × B0; for hydrogen γ/2π is about 42.58 MHz per tesla, so 1.5 T gives 63.87 MHz.
T1 weighting uses short TR and short TE; T2 weighting uses long TR and long TE.
Gradient coils encode position by slice selection, phase encoding and frequency encoding; RF coils transmit and receive the signal.
Ferromagnetic objects can become projectiles, so screening and controlled access are essential.
Check every implant against manufacturer labelling: MR safe, MR conditional or MR unsafe.
In pregnancy, avoid gadolinium unless essential and follow current national and local guidance.

en.title: Ultrasound: principles and practice
en.short: Sound waves, transducers, display modes, Doppler, artefacts, bioeffects and safe scanning skills.

sections.heading: Sound and probes
sections.text:
Ultrasound uses sound waves above human hearing, usually 2 to 15 MHz in diagnosis. A transducer contains piezoelectric crystals: a voltage makes them vibrate to send pulses, and returning echoes make a voltage. Gel couples the probe to skin.

Higher frequency gives shorter wavelength and better axial resolution, the ability to separate reflectors along the beam, but it is attenuated more and penetrates less. In soft tissue sound travels at about 1540 m/s.
Wavelength = speed ÷ frequency.
For 5 MHz: 1540 ÷ 5,000,000 = 0.000308 m, or 0.308 mm.

sections.heading: Modes and Doppler
sections.text:
Display modes present echoes. A-mode plots amplitude against depth. B-mode maps brightness as a 2D image and is the main mode. M-mode records motion along one line over time.

Doppler detects frequency shift from moving red cells; the shift depends on velocity, beam angle and frequency. Continuous wave Doppler has no depth selection; pulsed wave samples echoes in a small adjustable gate, so it can select depth. Colour Doppler overlays mean velocity and direction, and power Doppler shows flow presence with less angle dependence. A small beam-to-vessel angle improves velocity estimates.

sections.heading: Artefacts and safety
sections.text:
Artefacts are image features not matching anatomy. Acoustic shadowing is low signal behind strong reflectors such as bone or stones. Acoustic enhancement is brighter tissue behind fluid. Reverberation repeats echoes between strong reflectors. Mirror artefacts reflect across a strong interface.

Safety has thermal and mechanical effects. Heating rises with output and time; cavitation is bubble formation or collapse. Use ALARA, as low as reasonably achievable, and monitor the on-screen thermal index, which estimates heating, and the mechanical index, which estimates cavitation risk. B-mode is generally considered safe, but follow current national and World Health Organization guidance and local rules.

sections.heading: Operator skills
sections.text:
Operator skill shapes image quality. Confirm identity and indication, explain the procedure, and choose the correct probe and preset. Adjust gain, depth, focus and time gain compensation.

Scan in standard planes, keep the beam perpendicular to structures where possible, and record representative images. Recognise normal anatomy and your limits. Clean and check equipment, follow quality assurance, know your scope of practice.

keyPoints: Frequency and wavelength are linked by wavelength = speed ÷ frequency; in soft tissue speed is about 1540 m/s.
Higher frequency improves axial resolution but reduces penetration.
B-mode is the main 2D display; M-mode shows motion over time.
Doppler shift depends on blood velocity, beam angle and transmitted frequency.
Common artefacts include shadowing, enhancement, reverberation and mirroring.
Use ALARA and monitor thermal and mechanical indices; follow current national and WHO guidance.

en.title: Nuclear medicine and radionuclide imaging
en.short: Radiopharmaceuticals, gamma camera, SPECT and PET, uptake imaging, safety and limits.

sections.heading: Radiopharmaceuticals and uptake
sections.text:
A radiopharmaceutical is a radioactive tracer linked to a pharmaceutical that directs it to an organ or pathway. The radionuclide emits gamma rays or positrons; the pharmaceutical controls uptake. Technetium-99m is common: its half-life is about 6 hours and it emits 140 keV gamma rays. Fluorine-18 in fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) traces glucose use. Tracers are given in tiny amounts, so they do not act as drugs.

Uptake imaging shows function, such as how an organ takes up, traps or clears a tracer. A bone scan, for example, shows increased bone turnover, not a fracture line. This is teaching, not clinical advice; follow current national or WHO guidance and local protocols.

sections.heading: Gamma camera, SPECT and PET
sections.text:
The gamma camera detects gamma rays. A collimator admits near-parallel rays, forming an image but losing many photons. A scintillation crystal converts gamma rays to light, and photomultiplier tubes amplify and locate the signal. An energy window rejects scattered photons. Planar images show function with poor anatomical detail.

Single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) rotates the camera to reconstruct slices, often combined with CT. Positron emission tomography (PET) uses positron emitters: annihilation produces two 511 keV photons in opposite directions, and coincidence detection improves sensitivity. FDG PET shows glucose metabolism. A hot spot means increased uptake; a cold spot means reduced uptake. Infection and inflammation can also be hot.

sections.heading: Safety and limits
sections.text:
Patient care includes checking pregnancy and breastfeeding, explaining the test, encouraging hydration and voiding, and reducing anxiety. Radioactive patients can expose others, so apply local rules on time, distance and contact. Staff use shielding, dose monitoring and waste control.

The main limit is poor anatomical detail: small lesions may be missed, so choose the right test and combine with CT or MRI when needed. Protocols vary by country; check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Radiopharmaceuticals combine a radionuclide with a pharmaceutical that directs uptake.
Technetium-99m has a half-life of about 6 hours and emits 140 keV gamma rays.
The gamma camera uses a collimator, scintillation crystal, photomultiplier tubes and an energy window.
SPECT rotates a gamma camera; PET detects coincidence 511 keV annihilation photons.
Radionuclide images show function and have poor anatomical detail, so CT or MRI is often added.
Patient care and radiation safety include pregnancy checks, hydration, voiding, time, distance, shielding and waste control.

en.title: Mammography and breast imaging
en.short: Equipment, compression, positioning, screening and diagnostic roles, dose optimisation and quality assurance.

sections.heading: Equipment and technique
sections.text:
Mammography is X-ray imaging of the breast using a dedicated unit. It uses low-energy X-rays, a small focal spot, a compression paddle, a grid and automatic exposure control. The target and filter materials vary between units. Compression holds the breast still, spreads tissue, reduces thickness and lowers dose, but it must be applied firmly and kindly. The radiographer explains the procedure and protects privacy.

The standard views are craniocaudal (CC), from above, and mediolateral oblique (MLO), from an angle. Good MLO positioning includes the pectoral muscle, nipple in profile and the inframammary fold. Poor positioning is a common cause of repeats and missed tissue.

sections.heading: Screening and diagnosis
sections.text: Screening mammography images people without symptoms, aiming to find cancer early. Diagnostic mammography assesses symptoms such as a lump, or follows an abnormal screening result. It may add views, ultrasound or biopsy. Screening programmes differ by country in age range, interval, invitation system and funding. There is no single universal policy, so check current national guidance. The balance of benefit and harm is debated, and eligible people should receive clear information.

sections.heading: Dose and quality
sections.text:
Image quality depends on contrast, spatial resolution, noise, compression and positioning. Mean glandular dose (MGD) is the dose measure used in mammography. Dose optimisation means the lowest dose that gives a diagnostic image. For example, if one view gives an MGD of 1.2 mGy, four views give 4 × 1.2 = 4.8 mGy in total. These numbers are illustrative; real doses vary.

Quality assurance includes phantom images, compression checks, exposure and dose audits, artefact checks, monitor testing and staff training. Quality control tests are done at set intervals. Repeats should be recorded and reviewed.

keyPoints: Mammography uses a dedicated low-energy X-ray unit with compression and automatic exposure control.
Compression reduces breast thickness and dose, improves contrast and reduces motion.
CC and MLO are standard views; good MLO positioning includes pectoral muscle and nipple in profile.
Screening is for people without symptoms; diagnostic mammography assesses symptoms or abnormal results.
Screening policies differ by country, so check current national guidance.
MGD is the dose metric; total MGD is the sum of views, and quality assurance includes dose and image checks.

en.title: Pathology for medical imaging
en.short: How inflammation, infection, trauma, degeneration, vascular disease and cancer change imaging appearances.

sections.heading: Process to appearance
sections.text: Pathology explains why disease looks as it does on an image. Imaging detects changes in tissue density, water content, blood flow, cellular activity or structure. Plain films show bone and gas; CT shows density and enhancement; MRI shows soft tissue and water; ultrasound shows echoes and flow; nuclear medicine shows radiotracer uptake. Many appearances overlap; history and often biopsy decide diagnosis. Guidelines differ by country; check current national or WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Inflammation and infection
sections.text: Inflammation is the body’s response to injury or infection. Acute inflammation causes vessel widening and leakage, so tissue holds more water and blood. On CT it may look less dense; on fluid-sensitive MRI it is often bright; on ultrasound it may be swollen and darker (hypoechoic). Infection may form an abscess, a pus collection with an enhancing rim after contrast. Osteomyelitis may show bone destruction on plain film only after weeks, while MRI detects marrow oedema (fluid) earlier. Nuclear medicine can show increased uptake, but uptake is not specific.

sections.heading: Trauma and degeneration
sections.text: Trauma means injury. A fracture is a break in bone; plain film is often first, while CT shows fine fractures and organ injury. Bleeding forms a haematoma, blood collection, which may be dense on CT and change signal on MRI with time. Degeneration is gradual tissue wear. Osteoarthritis shows joint space narrowing, osteophytes (bony spurs), sclerosis and cysts on plain film. Disc degeneration shows loss of disc height and MRI signal. Age-related changes may cause no symptoms.

sections.heading: Vascular disease and neoplasia
sections.text: Vascular disease includes atherosclerosis (arterial plaque), aneurysm (dilated vessel) and infarction (tissue death from lost blood supply). CT or MR angiography and Doppler ultrasound show narrowing, dilation or clot. Neoplasia is abnormal new growth. Benign tumours stay local; malignant tumours invade and spread (metastasise). Imaging shows size, site, invasion and spread, but biopsy usually confirms type. Example: a man in Ibadan with painless blood in urine may have a bladder mass on ultrasound, then CT staging; schistosomiasis is a risk in endemic areas.

keyPoints: Imaging shows the physical consequences of disease, and many appearances overlap, so history and often biopsy decide the diagnosis.
Inflammation increases tissue water and blood; it may be less dense on CT, bright on fluid-sensitive MRI and darker (hypoechoic) on ultrasound.
An abscess often has an enhancing rim after contrast, and MRI detects osteomyelitis earlier than plain film.
CT is useful for fine fractures and organ injury after trauma, while haematoma density and MRI signal change with time.
Osteoarthritis shows joint space narrowing, osteophytes and sclerosis on plain film, and disc degeneration shows loss of disc height and MRI signal.
Vascular disease shows narrowing, dilation or clot on angiography or Doppler ultrasound, and neoplasia is staged by imaging but confirmed by biopsy.

en.title: Image interpretation and clinical reasoning
en.short: A routine for reading images, spotting variants and artefacts, and knowing when and how to refer.

sections.heading: A viewing routine
sections.text: Start by checking patient identity, the clinical question and the projection. Then judge image quality: exposure, positioning, motion and whether the whole area is shown. Use the same order every time, for example soft tissues, bones, joints, and the edges of the image. Compare with previous images when available. A systematic approach means repeating this routine so that a small finding is not missed. Clinical reasoning means combining the image with the history, examination and local guidance.

sections.heading: Variants and artefacts
sections.text: A normal variant is a harmless difference in appearance, such as an accessory ossicle, a sesamoid bone or a normal skin fold. Learn the common variants for each body part so you do not call them disease. An artefact is a feature caused by equipment, processing, clothing, jewellery or movement, not by the patient’s anatomy. Examples include grid lines, detector marks, motion blur and clothing creases. Artefacts can hide or mimic abnormality. If an image is inadequate, repeat it only under local policy and with radiation protection in mind.

sections.heading: Findings and referral
sections.text: Common abnormalities include fracture, dislocation, infection, obstruction, mass and foreign body.
