Describe what you see: position, size, shape, density and effect on nearby structures. Avoid naming a diagnosis unless you are sure. Case: Aminat, 24, has ankle pain after a fall. The image shows soft tissue swelling and a dark line at the lateral malleolus. Growth plates are normally closed at 24, so this is suspicious for fracture, not a normal variant. The radiographer records the finding, follows local policy and alerts the clinician; a radiologist or reporting radiographer then writes the formal report. Refer promptly if a finding is urgent, unexpected, outside your scope or you are unsure.

sections.heading: Scope and accountability
sections.text: Radiographer reporting varies by country. In some places radiographers give a preliminary opinion or a red dot alert; in others they write formal reports after extra training. Know your national law, employer policy and personal competence. Accountability means you are responsible for what you record, say and omit. Document the finding, the action taken and whom you informed. If you are unsure, ask. Do not use a report to replace clinical assessment. Guidelines change, so check current national or World Health Organization guidance.

keyPoints: Use the same viewing routine every time: check details and clinical question, image quality, all structures, and previous images.
Normal variants are common and harmless; artefacts come from equipment, processing or the patient and must not be mistaken for disease.
Describe findings clearly and compare with earlier images; uncertain or urgent findings need prompt discussion with a radiologist or clinician.
Know your local scope of practice and reporting policy; do not report beyond your competence or legal limits.
Record what you saw, what you did and whom you told, because accountability includes communication.
Clinical reasoning combines the image with history, examination and local guidance; this summary is education, not medical advice.

en.title: Quality assurance and imaging equipment
en.short: Quality control, acceptance testing, calibration, maintenance and audit of X-ray, CT, MRI and ultrasound equipment.

sections.heading: Quality assurance
sections.text: Quality assurance (QA) is the planned system that keeps imaging equipment safe, accurate and reliable. It includes quality control (QC), the routine tests that check performance against agreed limits. Acceptance testing happens after installation or major repair: the equipment is checked against the purchase specification and manufacturer’s data before clinical use. Commissioning confirms it is set up for local working practice. QA covers X-ray tubes and generators, CT scanners, MRI systems, ultrasound probes and other imaging devices.

sections.heading: Tests and calibration
sections.text: QC tests are usually simple, repeatable checks: radiation output, beam quality, collimation, image uniformity, noise, resolution and safety interlocks. For CT, checks include image quality and radiation dose indicators. For MRI, checks include signal-to-noise, uniformity and safety systems. For ultrasound, checks include image quality and probe condition. Calibration compares an instrument’s readings with a recognised metrology standard, so its accuracy is known and traceable. It is not the same as adjustment. Records must show the date, test, result, limits, action taken and the person responsible.

sections.heading: Maintenance and audit
sections.text: Maintenance is planned preventive work, such as cleaning, software updates, replacing worn parts and safety checks, plus corrective repair after a fault. A fault log and handover note help staff stop using unsafe equipment and report it. Audit compares practice with standards: are QC tests done on time, records complete, and faults closed? Standards come from national regulations, manufacturer specifications and professional guidance. Requirements differ by country and change, so check current national regulator or World Health Organization guidance.

sections.heading: Radiographer’s role
sections.text: Radiographers carry out or record many QC checks, recognise when images or equipment seem wrong, and remove unsafe equipment from use. They document results and escalate faults. Case: a radiographer notices CT images look noisier than usual and the dose indicator has drifted. They repeat the QC test, check the record, stop non-urgent scanning if needed, and inform medical physics or engineering. They do not adjust equipment beyond their training. This keeps patients and staff safe and supports reliable diagnosis.

keyPoints: Quality assurance is the planned system that keeps imaging equipment safe, accurate and reliable.
Quality control tests are routine checks of performance against agreed limits.
Acceptance testing checks new or repaired equipment against the specification before clinical use.
Calibration compares an instrument’s readings with a traceable standard so its accuracy is known.
Maintenance includes planned preventive work and corrective repair; audit compares practice with standards.
Radiographers record QC results, stop unsafe equipment and escalate faults within their training.

en.title: Professional practice, law and ethics in radiography
en.short: Consent, confidentiality, accountability, registration and ethical decisions in imaging practice.

sections.heading: Consent and confidentiality
sections.text: Consent is a person’s voluntary agreement to an examination or treatment after receiving enough information. Valid consent requires capacity, relevant information and freedom from pressure. For imaging, explain the procedure, its benefits and risks, alternatives, and what happens to images. Consent may be written, spoken or implied, depending on the local rule and the procedure; check your national framework. Confidentiality means keeping personal health information private. Share it only with those who need it for care, and follow national data protection law. Images and reports are health records, not ordinary pictures.

sections.heading: Registration and accountability
sections.text: Registration is official recognition that a person may practise a protected profession. Regulators set standards, keep a register and handle fitness to practise cases. Examples include the Health and Care Professions Council in the United Kingdom and the Radiographers Registration Board of Nigeria; your country may have a different body. Accountability means being answerable for your actions and omissions. Keep accurate records, work within your competence and scope, and report errors or unsafe practice. Registration usually requires continuing professional development, and rules change, so check the current requirements.

sections.heading: Ethical decisions and local law
sections.text: Ethics helps when rules do not give a clear answer. Common principles are autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice. They can conflict. Case: Chidi has a chest X-ray. His brother asks the radiographer whether Chidi has tuberculosis. The radiographer should not disclose without Chidi’s consent. She explains confidentiality, offers to speak with Chidi, and shares information only with the care team as needed. If Chidi lacks capacity, follow the national law and local policy on best interests. Law and professional codes differ between countries and change over time. Always check your own regulator’s current code and national legislation.

keyPoints: Valid consent needs capacity, information and voluntariness.
Explain benefits, risks, alternatives and use of images before imaging.
Keep patient information confidential and share it only on a need-to-know basis.
Registration is country-specific, so check your national regulator and current rules.
Accountability means accurate records, competence, scope of practice and reporting errors.
When duties conflict, use ethical principles and local law, and seek advice.

en.title: Advanced medical imaging physics
en.short: Reconstruction, quantification, dose optimisation and artefacts across CT, MRI, ultrasound and nuclear medicine.

sections.heading: Advanced reconstruction
sections.text: Modern scanners reconstruct images by solving an inverse problem: estimating the object from measured signals. CT uses filtered back projection or iterative and model-based methods that model photon statistics and system geometry. MRI uses parallel imaging, compressed sensing and non-Cartesian sampling. Ultrasound uses beamforming, harmonic and compounding methods. Nuclear medicine uses ordered-subset expectation maximisation (OSEM) with resolution recovery; PET also uses time-of-flight. These methods reduce noise or scan time but can alter texture and quantitative values, so validation matters.

sections.heading: Quantitative imaging
sections.text: Quantitative imaging measures a physical or biological property, not just appearance. CT uses Hounsfield units (HU), calibrated with water and air; dual-energy CT can separate materials. MRI maps T1, T2 and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC). Ultrasound elastography estimates tissue stiffness. PET/CT standardised uptake value (SUV) normalises activity concentration by injected activity and body size. Each metric needs a defined protocol, calibration and repeatability check before clinical or research use.

sections.heading: Dose and performance
sections.text: Dose optimisation keeps diagnostic information adequate while reducing exposure. CT uses volume CT dose index (CTDIvol) and dose-length product (DLP). Effective dose is approximate: E = DLP × k, where k is a region and age specific coefficient. Example: DLP 600 mGy·cm with k = 0.015 mSv/(mGy·cm) gives E = 9 mSv. MRI limits specific absorption rate (SAR); ultrasound uses thermal and mechanical indices; nuclear medicine controls administered activity. Performance is assessed with phantoms: modulation transfer function (MTF), noise power spectrum (NPS), detective quantum efficiency (DQE), contrast-to-noise ratio and reproducibility. Diagnostic reference levels (DRLs) guide local review; national and WHO or IAEA guidance changes.

sections.heading: Artefacts compared
sections.text: Artefacts reveal modality physics. CT shows beam hardening, photon starvation and motion. MRI shows chemical shift, susceptibility, wrap and radiofrequency artefacts. Ultrasound shows speckle, shadowing and reverberation. Nuclear medicine shows attenuation, scatter and partial-volume loss. Recognising the mechanism guides correction, protocol change or rejection of a non-diagnostic study.

keyPoints: Iterative and model-based reconstruction can reduce noise or scan time but may change image texture and quantitative values.
HU, T1, T2, ADC, elastography and SUV are quantitative only when protocol, calibration and repeatability are controlled.
CT dose indices are CTDIvol and DLP, where DLP = CTDIvol × scan length, and effective dose is estimated as E = DLP × k.
MRI safety limits include SAR; ultrasound uses thermal and mechanical indices; nuclear medicine limits administered activity.
Performance tests use phantoms and metrics such as MTF, NPS, DQE and contrast-to-noise ratio.
Artefact patterns differ by modality and point to the underlying physics, so compare CT, MRI, ultrasound and nuclear medicine before correcting.

en.title: Research methods and dissertation in radiography
en.short: Design, sampling, statistics, ethics and writing for a radiography dissertation.

sections.heading: Design and sampling
sections.text: Research design is the plan for answering a clear question. Quantitative designs include cross-sectional surveys, cohort and case-control studies, and experiments. Qualitative designs explore experience and meaning. Sampling is how participants are chosen. Probability methods, such as simple random, systematic, stratified and cluster sampling, reduce selection bias. Non-probability methods, such as convenience and purposive sampling, are common in radiography projects but limit generalisation. Sample size depends on the question, expected effect, variability and power; calculate it with a statistician or recognised software.

sections.heading: Methods and statistics
sections.text: Quantitative methods measure variables, for example image quality scores or waiting times. Qualitative methods use interviews, focus groups or observation and analyse themes. Statistics describe data with frequencies, means, medians and standard deviation. Inferential tests estimate whether a result is likely by chance; a p value is the probability of the data if the null hypothesis is true, not the size or importance of an effect. Report confidence intervals. In a diagnostic accuracy study of 200 patients, 40 had disease. The index test (the test being evaluated) was positive in 36 of them, so sensitivity = 36 ÷ 40 = 0.90, or 90%. Of 160 without disease, 140 tested negative, so specificity = 140 ÷ 160 = 0.875, or 87.5%.

sections.heading: Ethics and appraisal
sections.text: Ethics approval is required before data collection. Obtain informed consent, protect confidentiality, anonymise images and reports, store data securely, and follow national data protection and institutional rules. Declare conflicts. Critical appraisal asks whether the question, design, sampling, measurement and analysis support the conclusions, and whether bias or confounding could explain the result.

sections.heading: Writing the dissertation
sections.text: Plan a proposal with background, aim, methods, analysis plan, timeline and budget. Keep a data trail. Write the dissertation in a clear structure: introduction, methods, results, discussion and conclusion. Report limitations honestly and follow relevant reporting guidelines.

keyPoints: A clear research question determines design, sampling and analysis.
Probability sampling reduces selection bias; non-probability sampling limits generalisation.
A p value is not a measure of effect size; report confidence intervals.
Sensitivity = true positives ÷ all with disease; specificity = true negatives ÷ all without disease.
Obtain ethics approval, informed consent and secure anonymised data before collection.
Appraise bias, confounding and applicability, and keep an audit trail for the dissertation.

en.title: Artificial intelligence in medical imaging
en.short: Machine learning basics, validation, bias, regulation and the radiographer’s role in imaging AI.

sections.heading: Learning from images
sections.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) means computer systems performing tasks that normally need human intelligence. Machine learning (ML) is a branch of AI where algorithms learn patterns from data instead of being programmed rule by rule. In supervised learning, labelled images teach a model to map input to output, such as 'pneumothorax present' or 'normal'. Deep learning uses layered neural networks and can learn image features directly. A model is not a diagnosis; it is a statistical tool dependent on its training data and intended use.

sections.heading: Training and validation
sections.text: Data are split into training, validation and test sets. Training fits the model; validation tunes settings; the test set estimates performance on unseen images and must not be used for tuning. Overfitting is memorising training images and failing on new ones. External validation uses images from another hospital, scanner or population. Report sensitivity, specificity and confidence intervals, not accuracy alone.

sections.heading: Bias and limits
sections.text: Bias means systematic error that favours some groups or settings. It can enter through who is in the dataset, how labels were made, scanner differences and work practices. A tool trained mostly on one age group, sex or body size may perform worse elsewhere. Automation bias is over-trusting a computer suggestion. Radiographers should question outputs that conflict with the image and clinical context, and record discrepancies.

sections.heading: Regulation and role
sections.text: AI software used for diagnosis or triage is usually regulated as a medical device, but rules differ by country. Check the current national regulator and World Health Organization guidance; do not assume a CE mark (European Union), UKCA mark (United Kingdom) or FDA clearance (United States) covers local use. Clinical integration needs workflow fit, training, audit and human oversight. The radiographer checks patient identity, image quality and intended use, uses the tool as an aid, escalates concerns and reports errors. Example: a chest radiograph triage tool flags a possible pneumothorax; the radiographer confirms image quality, alerts the radiologist and documents the action.

keyPoints: Supervised machine learning learns from labelled images; deep learning learns features through layered neural networks.
Use separate training, validation and test sets, and keep the test set untouched.
Overfitting is memorising training data; external validation tests whether a model transfers to new settings.
Bias can come from datasets, labels, scanners and populations, while automation bias is over-trusting the tool.
AI for diagnosis or triage is generally regulated as a medical device; check current national and WHO guidance.
Radiographers verify identity, image quality and intended use, keep human oversight and report errors.
